units.text: 3. The taxonomy

No published taxonomy answers the question this spec asks. The academic taxonomies of agents read for it (2024 to 2026) classify by architecture, control structure, interaction type, autonomy, environment, memory and domain; none has an axis for where the compute runs and who pays for it (Inferred from the dozen read, not a systematic review; research note 13). Industry categories moved in 2025 and 2026 from assistants to agents: Gartner's 2025 report was a Magic Quadrant for AI Code Assistants (Reported, from a news digest), and a single secondary page, possibly machine-written, reports a 2026 Magic Quadrant for Enterprise AI Coding Agents (Reported). Thoughtworks' Technology Radar Vol 34 (April 2026) named "agent-native project memory and task tracking" a new category, with Beads as its example, put a small team of coding agents in Assess and coding agent swarms in Caution (Reported, from a dataset of the radar). The CNCF landscape has an AI Agent category with eleven subcategories, none for coding agents or for coordinating them (Verified, landscape.yml).
The taxonomy below keeps the axes that recur in that literature and adds the one it lacks. An axis earns its place only if it separates the neighbors in section 5.
Axis
Categories
Built on
Stack layer
L0 model; L1 single-agent harness (Claude Code, Codex CLI); L2 agent framework or SDK; L3 coordination layer; L4 execution platform (sandbox, CI, HPC scheduler, hosted service); L5 domain workflow
The CNCF landscape; Sapkota et al. 2025; Anthropic's split of harness and sandbox
Autonomy, by the human's role
Operator, collaborator, consultant, approver, observer
Feng, McDonald and Zhang 2025; the SE 3.0 levels of Hassan et al. 2025
Control topology
Single agent; orchestrator and workers; hierarchy of planners; decentralized peers; shared medium (blackboard, ledger)
Guo et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2025; Anthropic's patterns
Communication medium
Direct messages (mailboxes, A2A); context protocol (MCP); shared task list or blackboard; traces in the work itself (issues, branches, labels); tuple space
Yang et al. 2025; Gelernter 1985; Nii 1986; Heylighen 2016 on stigmergy
Concurrency control over shared work
Partitioning only (file ownership); lock; lease (a lock with expiry, renewal and a fence); optimistic (private copy, validate at merge, retry); hybrid
Kung and Robinson 1981; Gray and Cheriton 1989; Chubby, 2006
Dependencies managed
Shared resource; prerequisite; transfer; usability; simultaneity; task and subtask
Malone and Crowston 1994
Execution environment
Developer machine; vendor cloud; CI runner; HPC batch job; self-hosted server
Guo et al.; Suter et al. 2025; GitHub's runner docs
Trigger and lifetime
Interactive; event-driven; scheduled; batch; long-running loop or durable execution
Suter et al.; the two modes of claude-code-action
State and memory
Stateless; context window; session log; project memory files; shared work ledger; lineage record
Sapkota et al.; CNCF State and Memory; Beads
Cost model and payer
Inference: metered API, flat subscription, vendor credits; compute: own machine, vendor, free CI minutes, institution's allocation; licence: open, open core, proprietary
New here, from GitHub's billing pages and Anthropic's pricing
Verification and governance
None; self-check; model as judge; deterministic gates (tests, required checks, formal methods); human approval; external certification
MAST; Thoughtworks' feedback sensors; Hassan et al.'s Merge-Readiness Packs
Domain and maturity
Software engineering task; scientific workflow; research software by kind, use and readiness level; business process
Liu et al. 2024; Suter et al.; the GI and de-RSE guideline after Hasselbring et al. 2024

Three axes carry this study. Axis 10 is where the Actions story lives and the one no taxonomy has. Axis 5 is where Symphony's claim sits: a claim made by creating a branch, a lease-like release and optimistic merging. Axis 11 is where Beethoven's claim sits: a tool, never a model, decides. Axes 1, 3 and 7 locate the neighbors.

The classical frames fit closely. Malone and Crowston define coordination as "managing dependencies among activities" and name four families of dependency, one of which, producer and consumer, splits into prerequisite, transfer and usability (Reported, from mirrors of the paper; research note 13). Each of the six kinds has a counterpart in agent work: claiming an issue is a shared resource, a blocker is a prerequisite, a pull request is a transfer, a required check is a usability standard, the landing order of overlapping work is simultaneity, and an epic is task and subtask (Inferred; research note 13).
